content.content:
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.


Print the curator's message(s) at a UTC timestamp or its prefix, verbatim.

    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53          # every message of his in that minute
    python3 -I show.py 2026-10-12T15:53:07.5     # a finer prefix
    python3 -I show.py --list 2026-10-12         # one line per message (timestamp, source, length, start)
    python3 -I show.py --count                   # how many messages the three sources give

A prefix may use a space instead of the T and may end in Z. All times are UTC.

His messages come from three places, and the header of each printed message says which:
  main  the main-session lines of the transcripts in /root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/
        and /home/user/fortress-transcripts-blinded/projects/-home-user-fortress/ (the .parts
        folders included): `user` lines that are not isMeta, not sidechain, with text content
        that does not start with '<' and is not a compaction summary; deduplicated by uuid,
        because a resumed transcript replays earlier lines.
  s1    the same lines of the first coordinating session (bdff267d), read with `git show` from
        the `transcripts` branch (origin/transcripts) of this repository, 2026-08-18 to 2026-09-17.
        Skipped, with a note on stderr, if that branch is not in the clone.
  queued  a message he queued while an agent was busy that no `user` line holds as its text
        (the queue-operation `enqueue` lines and the queued_command attachments); its time is the

Yes, it makes sense. Here is what I hear you asking, part by part, then answers to the two direct questions, then how I would produce it.

**What you are asking for.** One document, a map of the territory, written before the sealed tree is opened. It has these parts:

1. **Repository architecture.** The modules in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/` and the top-level directories, each with its role and what it depends on. The repo already has a partial version of this in `explorations/repo-internals.md`; the map either extends it or supersedes it.
2. **Language architecture, spec to implementation.** For each feature area of the latest committed spec (not the 1.0 frozen one), where it lives: in the parser, in the static checker, in the interpreter, in the compiler, in the shipped library, or nowhere. The particular question you named: what enables the numeric tower. The tower is library code, but it stands on traits, generic types, operator overloading and dispatch, and those are language mechanisms implemented in the checker and runtime. The map separates enabling blocks from things built on them.
3. **The compile pipeline, phase by phase.** Rats! parser produces the AST; grammar extensions are expanded; desugaring; type checking; bytecode generation with ASM; the runtime class loader that generates code on the fly; the Java interop surface. For each phase: which module, what it produces, what the next phase needs from it. You are right that there is Java interop, the `nativeHelpers` module and the compiler's `NativeHelper` bindings are that surface.
4. **Test coverage.** Which test directories exercise which layer, whether the interpreter and compiler suites are shared or separate, and how much of each layer has no test at all. This decides how safely each layer can be modified.
5. **Gaps on the path.** Of the 309 ledger rows, which ones sit on the road from today's tree to a fast compiled microgpt, in dependency order, and what breaks if each is left alone.
6. **The development loop.** What makes an iteration slow, which of those costs are ledger rows already, and which are tooling.
7. **A dependency map.** Touching this affects that, so that fixes are ordered and the artifact does not fall apart under edits.

**The guiding constraint you stated.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the latest spec, not redesign the language. The measuring stick is one program: microgpt compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microgpt later gives the floor to aim at.

**The phase boundary you described.** Tag the tree at the unsealing point, then start the next phase: modifying the original sources, with lessons from the explorations. The map is the last prep before that tag.

**Terminology: gate.** A gate is the check a change must pass before it is accepted. Ours has been the fully green suite: `ant testFast` plus `ant testSystem`. The map's coverage part tells us where that gate is blind.

**Fortify and Fortick, answered.** Fortify is an Emacs Lisp program, `Fortify/fortify.el`, 8,024 lines, plus a LaTeX style file. It rewrites Fortress source into LaTeX commands so the spec and papers show code as typeset math. It runs from `bin/fortify` or an Ant task. Fortick is a wrapper script that takes a document with backtick-delimited Fortress snippets and replaces them with the fortified form. Neither touches the language, parser, or runtime. The separate `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. We would touch Fortify only if we changed the spec's LaTeX build or wanted the microgpt article typeset that way. Given your verdict on the notation, that is a no. Your verdict itself I record as a position: the 2D rendering is presentation, not language, and not on our path.

**One correction to your picture.** The Unicode operators and mathematical spelling are in the language itself. Fortress source can be written with `∑`, `∈`, `×` and juxtaposition directly, and the ASCII spellings are aliases the parser accepts. Fortify only adds the typesetting on top. So dropping Fortify loses nothing on our path.

**How I would produce the map.** Survey work goes to Opus workers, one brief per part where it needs reading of code or counting of tests: the module and phase walk (parts 1 and 3), the spec-to-implementation table (part 2), and the test coverage census (part 4). Parts 5 to 7 are design and stay in this thread, built on the ledger and the three survey reports. The map lives in `explorations/coordinator/` beside FACTS and POSITIONS, since it is the thing read at every session start from the next phase on.

On your word, the three survey workers start.

<!-- The curator's decisions about the project (the language, the library, the tree and its tools, the specification and the plan) as they stand now. One line per entry under its permanent number, `- P-48 **Title.** Text.`, written only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`. `POSITIONS-history.md` holds each change's provenance and the line as it stood before. What an entry holds and how it is written: the `coordinator` skill, `references/record.md`. How the curator and the coordinator work is that skill's, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast.** The judge is `Specification/`, the Working Draft of February 2011 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it (P-25). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states the revival's changes (P-95). The floor to measure against is a pure-Java microGPT, not yet written (PLAN phase 6).
- P-8 **Where the designers left no word, he decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** He accepts the language's unfinished corners rather than stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and takes the designers to have known more than he does. So a review checks his decisions against their intent, for errors of commission and of omission; its items are decisions in this file. Detail: `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md`, "In short".
- P-9 **The search is for microGPT's most readable expression.** In his words, "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." The two sources are Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation, with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms. The flat program in Hsu's style, C4, fell short, so polishing happens in the vocabulary, the operations the model is written in. C4 is the APL program's target form. Its hyperparameters are tuple bindings, the form an APL strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form of those lines is set aside.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its remaining ground, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, is not pursued.** Its sub-language expands APL to Fortress code over native arrays, and its APL microGPT program stays in the walk check (P-30).
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless he asks.** Fortify's mathematical rendering bakes one view of a computation into the syntax, though the same mathematics can be written many ways. APL's one glyph for each transformation does that better. It is presentation only, off the path, and no argument for Fortress.
- P-12 **The type checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over.** He wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs, and sees it as low-hanging fruit. Today it checks only against the compiler's prelude (F-9). It comes once walk also takes the static coercions that the checker inserts (P-59).

You didn't contradict anything. The checker as it landed in batch N contradicts your decision, and option 1 fixes the checker.

The example: `a: V = k(NOf(1))`, with two declarations of `k`.
- `k[\T extends N\](x: T): T` is generic. It fits the argument as it is, and returns an `N`.
- `k(x: V): V` is plain. It fits only if `NOf(1)` is first converted to `V`.
- The result must go into `a: V`, and an `N` can be converted to `V`.

Your decision 1 says a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. So the generic `k` should run, and its `N` result gets converted to `V` at the assignment. Walk does exactly that.

What the landed checker does:
1. Its first attempt matches without any conversion, but it also demands that the result already be a `V`. The generic's result is an `N`, so the generic is ruled out.
2. Its second attempt allows conversions and finds `k(V)`, by converting the argument.

So the compiled program runs `k(V)` and walk runs the generic. The two paths disagree, and the compiled one goes against your rule.

Option 1 reorders the first attempt: match without conversion and without demanding the result type, keep the winner if its result can be converted to `V`, and only then try conversions. That's your rule as written. It's one checker rung, in batch 8.

That's all there is to it. The audit's section 6, item 4 says the same in four lines.

## In short

- On every large call he has gone the way the designers' own implementers went: one library, the exclusion rule kept and the number tower flattened, sizes in the types with unboxed storage, the 2009 overload sentence dropped, `comprises` read at the level of values, conversions never changing which declaration runs. Each of these is what the type group built or wrote last, not what the early draft wished.
- Where the designers left no word, his calls are pragmatic, consistent with each other, and mostly in the library's own patterns. Two are not: row 330 (`floor` on a float returning an unbounded integer), decided on a premise route A then removed and against the library's consistent declaration; and the written `extends Object` bound of batch 7, which turned a compile-time refusal into a JVM crash the switch-over will meet (row 447).
- No cardinal error of commission. Row 330 has cost nothing yet and reverses for the price of one entry. Row 447 costs one code-generator rung and must land before the switch-over.
- The errors of omission are in the plan, not in the decisions: the switch-over (phase 4) is the largest and least designed piece; phase 5's collision between "no model line changes" and "sizes in the model's own types" is measured (decision D's diff: 21 lines out, 29 in) but not yet faced by him; the unboxed store's mechanism (decision A) has no design and the "fast" half of the goal rests on it.
- The standard itself has two voices on the tower, and his decisions follow the later one. The record's own brief for route A did not cite the sentence that most supports it (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:501-502`).
- He has not gone astray. Section 6 lists eleven things to decide or confirm, the first four before batch 7b.

....
## 1. Primer: what the designers were aiming for

Terms are defined where they first appear. "The team" is the Sun/Oracle Fortress group, 2003-2012. "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the static type checker, which runs only on the compiled path. "The one library" is the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`), which his decision of 2026-09-21 makes the library the compiler checks. "The prelude" is the compiler's own smaller library (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), to be deleted at "the switch-over", the day the compiled path reads the one library.

### The three texts, and which is the designers' latest word

- The 2008 release is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, 262 pages, the team's own artefact (`403afbe0b`, 2008-03-31).
- The Working Draft is the LaTeX under `Specification/`. The team's last edit to its text is 2010-12-09 (`44e03b176`). Steele cloned it whole into `Specification-1.0-frozen/` on 2012-01-04, so the frozen directory is byte for byte the draft of 2011-02-02, not the 1.0 text; only the PDF beside it is 1.0 (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 1-2, checked). "July 2012" on the revival's PDF is the date of a parentless import commit, chosen by the revival (`414b790e3`), not of any edit.
- The restart is `Documentation/Specification/`, begun 2012-02-20 by Luchangco, abandoned 2012-05-31 with most chapters empty. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, 1,056 lines) is fresh 2012 prose and the team's last word on types, exclusion and `comprises`. It has no chapter on static parameters, numbers, coercion beyond a relation, or the library.
- The papers: the OOPSLA 2011 type-system paper (`Papers/Types/`), Naden's 2012 journal text on the return-type rule (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, last touched 2012-08-31, the project's last day), the Welterweight calculus (2012), the four patents filed 2012-08-31, and Steele's 2016 retrospective (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`).
- So "the designers' latest word" is not one text. On types and the exclusion rule it is the 2012 Types chapter and Naden. On the library, static parameters, coercion, overloading resolution and the number chapters it is the Working Draft, whose text on those topics is 2008-2010. On what they actually made run, it is the code: the interpreter's library (2007-2012, never type-checked) and the compiler's prelude and checker (2009-2012).

....
### 10. Are the team's demos put back into the tree's running state? (tension with "one tree with everything running")

- 21 of 24 demos with an unwritten clause-form sum fail since the flat tower; no gate stage runs demos.
- Options: 1. A small rung respells the 21 with their static arguments, as the team's own tests write them, and a report-only demo stage joins the gate. Costs one rung. 2. Leave them until walk accepts an unwritten static argument (answer 7's later work).
- Recommendation: 1, when a batch has a free slot; not before batch 7b.

### 11. Is the goal's wording corrected? (F1)

- "The July 2012 draft" is the revival's label; the team's text is of December 2010, and it is revised in place with the 2012 Types chapter beside it.

You're close. Three corrections, then why `Any` isn't just the status quo.

**`Any` and `Bottom` are opposite ends.**
- `Any` is the top: every type sits below it, and every value in Fortress belongs to it.
- `Bottom` is the bottom: it sits below every type and has no values at all. It's the type of an expression that never returns a value, such as `throw`.
- The question in item 3 is only about the top. When a generic declaration writes `[\T\]` with no bound, what may `T` be?

**What `Object` is in Fortress.** It isn't Scala's `object` keyword, although Fortress has a similar keyword:
- A Fortress `object` declaration makes values. Without parameters it's a singleton, like Scala's `object`. With parameters, like `object Just[\T\](x: T)`, it's a constructor, much like a Scala case class. So your memory connects the right things.
- The type `Object` is the supertype of every value those declarations make.
- There are no Java-style primitives at the language level. `ZZ32`, `RR64` and `String` are all under `Object`. The unboxed `double` is only how the compiler may store an `RR64`.

**What `Any` has that `Object` doesn't:** tuples like `(ZZ32, ZZ32)`, functions like `ZZ32 -> ZZ32`, and the empty tuple `()`. In Fortress these are not objects. The 2012 Types chapter says the same: `Any` is the top, and `Object` excludes function types.

**Why `Any` isn't just the status quo:**
- The library's own design needs it. A two-dimensional array is indexed by a pair: `Array[\RR64, (ZZ32, ZZ32)\]`. A list of pairs is `List[\(K, V)\]`. Under `Object`, every generic container instantiated at a tuple would be refused. That was measured at 163 refusals, most of them tuple index types, including the arrays microGPT uses.
- The draft's sentence saying `Object` dates from 2008 to 2010, before the library instantiated generics at tuples everywhere. The 2012 Types chapter makes `Any` the top.
- The compile path currently writes `Object` for an empty bound (row 412), which is why it refuses generics at tuple types today. That divergence goes away at the switch-over.

So the choice is between the draft's 2008 wording and what the library needs and the designers' later text says. Option 1 writes `Any` into the specification with a callout recording that the draft said `Object`.

- **Integers into the 64-bit float `RR64`:** your rule was to convert only where it's exact, so you never silently lose precision. An `RR64` holds any integer up to 2^53 exactly. So `ZZ32` and integer numerals convert into `RR64` automatically, while `ZZ64`, whose values go past 2^53, needs an explicit `asFloat`.

# The three specification artefacts: what each one is, and how they relate

## Summary

- `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` is the real 1.0 release artefact: added
  2008-03-31 by the team (`403afbe0b`). The LaTeX **sources** sitting next to it in
  `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are not 1.0 text — they are a January 2012 clone of the
  then-current working draft, made by Guy Steele, and they are still today the working
  draft in 202 of 208 tracked files.
- `Specification/` is that same working draft, carried forward. The team's last edit to
  its text is 2010-12-09. Nobody touched it again until the revival built and committed
  a rendered PDF from it in 2026, under the label "July 19, 2012" — a date the revival
  chose, not the team, and not the date of any edit.
- `Documentation/Specification/` is a separate, later, unfinished restart: begun
  2012-02-20 by Victor Luchangco, restructured and substantially written by Steele and
  Luchangco through May 2012, abandoned on 2012-05-31 with a 65-page draft PDF and most
  chapters still empty skeletons. Two of its finished chapters (Types, and part of
  Lexical Structure) are, by date, newer team prose than anything in `Specification/`.

## 2. Why Steele froze the draft in January 2012

`c02fa44d0` ("Cloned Specification directory into Specification-1.0-frozen", Guy Steele,
2012-01-04) sits inside a week of intense work by David Chase and Jean-Baptiste Tristan
on operator static parameters and RTTI (`b24a48a3c`, `4305f45d9`, `5d1c1b5ce`,
`30b00ab60`, all 2012-01-04 to 01-13) — none of it touching the specification. Nothing in
the surrounding commit messages states a reason for the clone.

What the record does show is what happened *after*: the team never again edited
`Specification/`'s text (confirmed by the date-order tree walk below); instead, five and
a half weeks later, Victor Luchangco started a **different, new** directory,
`Documentation/Specification/` (`166841592`, 2012-02-20), and by May 2012 Steele had
joined him in restructuring and writing it (§3). Read against that sequence, the January
clone reads as Steele setting the existing draft aside — freezing it as a fixed
reference point — just before the team began rethinking the specification from scratch
rather than continuing to edit the old one. This is a reading of the sequence, not a
stated reason; no design note, README, or mailing-list text in the tree says so in words.
(`explorations/reviews/spec-change-form.md:237-239` reaches the same reading
independently: "Before a large revision (2012). Steele copied the whole directory ... and,
four months later, began a new document instead of editing the old one.")

The name "1.0-frozen" is misleading taken literally. `git diff --quiet
2f8b4331a:Specification c02fa44d0:Specification-1.0-frozen` succeeds (verified directly)
— the clone is byte-for-byte the working draft as it stood on 2011-02-02, not the 1.0
text. Today the two source trees still differ in only 5 of 208 tracked files: the
revival's restyling of `fortress/fortress.tex` and its three `fortress/*.pl` table
generators (`4672b71cd`), and one historical stray `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1`
line at `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17` that is absent from the frozen copy
(`explorations/coordinator/map/spec-to-implementation.md:109-111,117`). The only
genuinely-1.0 content near it is the PDF beside it (§1).

content.content:
2e33f4ab2 2026-09-16T23:19:49+00:00 Map: three more survey reports (modules and phases, spec to implementation, design-intent sources)

Where are Fortify and Fortick, and when would we touch them? `Fortify/fortify.el` (8,024 lines) plus `fortify.sty`, driven by `bin/fortify` and an Ant task; `bin/fortick` wraps it for backtick-delimited snippets in a document; `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. They are presentation only; nothing on either path depends on them (A.6, `design-intent-sources.md` §6, the notation row). The Unicode operators and juxtaposition are the language itself; Fortify only typesets them.

Which spec counts? `Specification/`, "Working Draft, July 19, 2012", revision 4267. The sources under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are a byte-identical copy of the same draft in 202 of 208 files; only the PDF beside them is the 1.0 artefact (`spec-to-implementation.md` §1.2). This corrects the FACTS entry that called the frozen tree "1.0".

## 4. Decisions the surveys put on the table

Part one of the map, `explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, covers the modules and the two pipelines; this part covers the specification and where each feature it defines is implemented. Where the two overlap (the dead top-level `CompilerLibrary/`, the prelude switch in `WellKnownNames`, the phase order) they were written independently and agree.

## 1. The specification that counts

The latest committed specification is `Specification/`; its root is `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex`, a `book` whose seven `\part` files are `\input` at `fortress.tex:149-155`.
